idiom_name: multiprocessing.shared_memory name hand-off (object-store key across hosts)
implementation_notes: Python has no framework-level claim check, so the structure is written around a store: multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory is the stdlib primitive that matches the pattern literally - one process creates the block (and can adopt ShareableList for structured data), another attaches to it by name, and only the name travels in the message, which removes pickling and copying from the boundary. Across hosts the same shape uses a UUID key plus an object store or a shared cache, and the Check Luggage step (extract, store, replace) plus the deletion rule (shm.unlink or a store-side TTL) are application code either way. The shared-memory form stays justified for large numeric buffers on one host, where serialising the same data into a pickle would double peak memory; for small messages the store hop is pure overhead.
code_sketch:
from multiprocessing import shared_memory

shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=len(payload))
shm.buf[:len(payload)] = payload
queue.send({"order_id": oid, "claim_check": shm.name})    # only the name travels
# consumer: shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(name=ref)
#           data = bytes(shm.buf[:size]); shm.close(); shm.unlink()
pitfalls: A SharedMemory block outlives its creator until someone unlinks it: a crash between create and unlink leaves the segment in /dev/shm, and later runs hit FileExistsError or silently attach to a stale block.

The name is only meaningful inside the same memory namespace, so a consumer on another host either fails to attach or finds an unrelated block of the same name - the message must not be treated as portable.
Size is fixed at creation and nothing synchronises access: the length must travel out of band, and concurrent writers need their own lock because shared memory is memory, not a channel.
